Spent my first hour learning the ropes - hunting and gathering - building shelter, my stash, clothes etc. Some guy came knocking at my shack. "Food please. Give me Food Please" is what he as he stared me down with his Bow. I thought to myself - "is this a stick up?".. so I closed my door. Waited 2 mins opened my door .. An Arrow whizzed past my head. I quickly shut the door. I waited another 3 mins and ran out the door, my bow equipped. That is when I seen the other 3 guys. All of them armed with Bows. I lasted about 10 seconds.
Spawned again - no idea where my shelter was. Spent another hour gathering until I finally gave up on my orignal shack and started building a fortress. Found a real nice place on the top of a really high hill. Figured easier to defend and can see bandits coming. Problem was - animals and resources were very scarce. Eventually gave up and exited server (after 4-5 hrs total)
Server 2. Tons of players, tons of resources, tons of zombies. Lots of structures and people seemed generally nice. Punched another 4 hours gathering and building. Locked my doors and logged out for the night. -- Next morning I logged back in to find the door to my building blown off and all my stuff gone. Essentially meaning - 4 hours the day before was for nothing.
After speaking to people currently on the server they came off to me as a bundle off @ssclowns.  Decided best to leave.
Server 3. A small amount of friendly people. Lots of Zombies and lots of resources. So far so good. I found myself a nice little spot up in the hills over looking the zombie camps and resources. Hoping this might work out better.  After making a little shelter and some improvements I locked my door once more and logged out. Hoping this time when I log back in everything will be as I left it.
At its current stage (alpha) I find it hard to recommend. Im having some fun but its a little stressful playing for hours and thinking "If I log out, when I come back my progress may be all gone" ...
Will update this as game gets updated as well.
UPDATE 1: (Feb 1st, 23 hours played)
I'm changing my recommend to a Yes. Reason being.. obviously Ive been playing the game more. Server 3 I mentioned above has been more fun. Most of the people are nice and no admin abuse. Have myself a nice little place started and have learned alot.
Joined a fourth server. One with a whole town of good people. The only rule is, if you kill within the town (and boundary) , there's a bounty on your head. So there is a safe haven while building within its gates. All bets are off though once you leave the town and hunt/gather etc. Very fun and much more balanced then previous servers. Only problem with this setup however is there is sometimes alot of lag in the town. Game isn't really meant to have that many structures in the one place.
This game is not however recommended for people that drop things quick. Its too easy to have my experience I listed above and uninstall forever. With as many games as I do and as little time, the acceptance with RUST "Nothing lasts forever .. or even between logins" is a MUST.

I think this is the future of gaming.  I hate it, but somehow I'm enthralled.  Why should I have fun taking my time beating on trees and animals and rocks with the threat of death looming in the background like some a hole laughing from above? But oh wait, just as I'm in the middle of farming, trying to survive with a piece of chicken that took me forever to aquire, I'm suddenly hit on the back of the head by some desperate soul who needed sustenance just as much as I did.  I can't blame him, even though I despise him.  He wanted what I did; to survive.  In a nut shell, that is what this game is about.  You begin to learn to protect yourself, never trust anyone, and never get too comfortable in your situation.  Hasn't this been done before in other games?  Certainly it has, but never with such a feeling of dread, a sense of revenge, and a motivation to NEVER let the same thing happen to you again.  This is Rust, and this is more than a game.  Or so it seems.

Its in Alpha.  So this is just a "For now" review as of 25 January 2014.
Rust is exactly the same as what DayZ plans to be but comes from a different initial development focus (world modification vs equipment variety).  Both will be like minecraft but gritty.  In Rust you punch trees with a rock to collect wood, punch rocks with a rock to get... rocks, and punch animals to get chicken and cloth (irrespective of animal species).  Now all of this seems like a mechanical foundation that will prove successful (just like Minecraft) except the variety and complexity of different types of material and building options just arent there yet.  Give it time so that you have to manage all the different types of meat and raw building materials and it will probably be more fun.  Plus hopefully give some variety to the utter sameness of the huts and area.  (Build a hut, add a door, walk 200 meters, spin in a circle for 30 seconds, and I dare you to find your hut again amongst all the exact clones)
The server wide chat mechanic is very strange in the environment leading to a lot of "Player884 is a haxor cheat" and "Aww, Player820 why did you kill me?" stuff.  This really breaks the immersion since part of the survival excitement is not knowing why people do what they do unless you actually communicate (before shooting or getting shot).  It also removes the feeling of isolation that I would expect (although the map is so small, the feeling may never really exist).  The location based voice chat works well.  I would love to see the server wide chat filtered on location so my comments are only visible to people who would be able to hear me speak over voice.  Not that I dont like knowing that "Player724 is KOS" since I wont be able to see his name tag until after he is close enough to shoot me.  KOS is apparently shorthand for Kill On Sight meaning either they will shoot you or everyone thinks you should shoot them.
I do appreciate the minecraft-style hyper day-night cycle that takes 10-15 minutes per.  Unlike minecraft, the world is not made up of resources.  Instead, resources (boulders, log piles, and animals) spawn randomly.  Morning is the prime time to collect since people cant see to gather during the dark cycle.  But of course, it is harder to see the zombie or bear and avoid a confrontation.  If day was actually 8 hours, you would only find resources once a day and leave a lot of people naked wielding stones.
All of your progress (if you have any) is tied to the server you play on.  But as far as I have seen, servers show up for a day then wink out to be replaced by other servers.  So for all my time playing, I have rarely benefitted from my previous play sessions.  But I am pretty efficient at getting the basics accomplished now.  Again, this is most likely an affect of early access status and I would expect it to settle down on a feature complete release.
I think this game is a good one to watch over the next year or so.  It has gobs of potential if it can continue to expand it's already working set of functionality.
*** UPDATE Same Day ***
After you die, you can still hear the audio of anyone near you when you died.  I found this incredibly frustrating.  Not only is it a poor simulation (dead people don't hear) but this person whom I could hear (but I could not communicate with) absolutely loathed me.  He was convinced I had done some horrible things to him and he took the time to exult in his achievement.  This 10 second exchange was absolutely chilling for me.  I don't mind so much getting killed senselessly, but the mean-hearted personally targeted feeling of it stuck with me.

I played it for near 15 Hours now and im at a Point where i say, "Im finished with it, there is not much to see for me any more".  If you're searching for a playable Survival Game i wouldn't  recommend you to buy it, because it's nowhere near finished. Also i want to warn you that the game in it's current state feels more like a KoS (Kill on Sight ) game, if you are not playing on a pure PvE Server with just a few people (max 20) you will meet alot of other Players, and they will try to kill you, guaranteed. I made once the Mistake and helped a guy screaming for help,  and let him in, he tried to kill me luckily i won but that is just one example. Also the spawning system is not that great, in the first night(s) you need to find pigs/Chicken or you will starve, and you got absolutely no influence where you spawn. I must admit it took me atleast 5 lifes to get really started, because you need to be in a decent location with Animals around and stone/wood logs. Having no (ingame) map doesn't help also, even though i actually enjoyed it  after a certain point. With time you really can recognize the environment, but i used a map of Rust which i found on the internet (and which i will link at the end of the review) which helped me to somewhat know in which direction i need to go and what kind of resources are in certain areas and just to know where i am in general. I know that all sounds  very negative, but i can see where the game is heading, and the atmosphere is actually really great. So if you want to have influence in an upcoming Survival title with alot of Potential and/or want to try it now since you will buy it later anyway, go for it.

In an era that mixes the hunter/gather society and the modern era - there is much to do in Rust. When you take your first breath on the island of Rust, opening up your eyes - you are met with a rock in which you have the urge to name Wilson. You look around, born into this world with nobody else, so you take it that you too must be family of this rock, that it was this rock that gave you life, that you are a rock, and you must be as naked as the rock you're holding. You eventually figure out that you can swing the rock and decide to see what happens if you swing it at a bear. Not good. As you find out Wilson isn't strong enough. You become nearly dead. Bleeding.
Suddenly, you hear a high-piercing noise ring through the air, into the bear's skull. It's dead. You turn around and get a glimps of an object who can stand on two legs, covered in what looks like bear fur. It's obviously not a rock, and doesn't hold a rock like you do. Instead, it looks like he is holding a black stick, a black and shiny stick, with a hole at the tip and funny things sticking out of it.
The strange object vocalizes, saying something you can understand:
"Nice d1ck f@66ot!"
The last thing you hear was the same sound you heard before the collapse of the bear. You're dead. You're p15sed. You must learn how to build a shiny black stick such as that object's. You must get your revenge.

The game is great in concept, but if you want to actually get anywhere in the game you need to be playing with a group of players or on a No PVP server. The game is absolutely unforgiving to the new person playing by themselves. I feel the game would benefit from modified servers that would allow you to turn personal PVP mode on and off as you please.
One must first figure out exactly what they want to do with the game before they pick the server they play on. For instance I was playing on a PVP enabled server with large population. After 15 hours of farming and building up a relatively nice structure, the server started getting ddosed and thrown into rubber band mode. Running back to my base and opening my door was a pain, however the 6 second delay on closing the door was worse, cos as soon as my client resolved I had someone standing infront of me slicing my face open with an axe, being locked in was not an issue for the guy seeing as he must have had C4 or a friend with some nearby. Back to square one again after losing 15 hours worth of a build made me lose my mind and rage quit the server, despite having active and friendly admins. If you get invested in what you create and play on a pvp server... just prepare for some major upsets along the way.
In summary, I will definitely be playing this game again, and look forward to how the alpha progresses. I just don't think i will ever trust another player in the game again, and that sort of saps some of the enjoyment out of it. You could build some awesome things if you just worked together, but instead we're all just rabid dogs frothing at the mouths, snapping at any scrap of meat that comes nearby, do not play if you care about your game progression.

I, like many others, put down US$20 in order to alpha-test this new survival game, which is loosely based on DayZ. The inherent issues with Early Access games such as this is that they implement only the bare essentials, and they’re asking you to pay in order to play what could be considered, at its best, unfinished/unpolished gameplay, and at its worse, a pointless waste of time.
To date, I have sunk 38 hours of my life attempting to make some progress, any progress, playing this game online with other people. Most of that time was spent collecting sparsely generated resources in an incredibly large environment, while trying in vain to avoid being killed by other overpowered players during that process. I wasn’t alone either, I worked with my loving partner, who I convinced to buy the game in order to properly try it out.
The problem with RUST lies in the core concept of the game: it rewards those who are already geared up and leaves new players grinding for hours on end in out of the way areas with little to no available resources, only to eventually be ripped off by the more powerful players. In short, the game has incredibly bad balance, and this doesn’t seem to be a major concern for either the developers or those who currently play the game.
Time after time, we tried to collect resources in order to reach the level that the others players were already at. Nine times out of ten we would run into another player who is fully loaded within the first few minutes of a new spawn, where they would instantly kill us for no reason; well before we could even build a rudimentary stone hatchet. On the rare occasions where we managed to evade detection and stay alive for a few hours, we would manage to build a base, only to be killed and looted before any real progress was made. Any attempts to object to the situation would be shrugged off by loaded players with “Welcome to RUST”, or even more obscenely, “Suck♥♥♥♥♥♥ that’s how the game is played”.
What’s going on here is more problematic than you may think. The game rewards players in a better position, and even encourages them to go around griefing new players, mainly because there is absolutely nothing left to do once you reach that “all-powerful” point. The players get so bored, they go looking for trouble in order to justify their position and the money that they have spent on a game with no goals left to pursue. The ones who pay for this design flaw are new players, which is completely contrary to proper game development.
Nobody wants to spend six hours grinding for resources, just to be killed and required to start from scratch again. As I said, I’ve wasted 38 hours already and still haven’t managed to get past building a base. You may just think I am upset that I never managed to get anywhere, and that may be true, but I am myself an open source game developer, and if the games I made behaved in this manner, people would complain and probably stop playing entirely.
The biggest reason for RUST’s success is the “brand name” the developers brings to it, Garry Newman and Facepunch studios. This game is not popular because it is good, per se; it is popular for the sake of being popular, and it brings with it an entirely undesirable player base, all of whom get kicks from hacking, griefing, lording over the weak, and causing all manner of trouble. In time, this will limit the number of players who are actually playing the game to the elitist few; sales are not an accurate representation of how good a game really is.
It is insane that a game this broken continues to receive rave reviews and massive amounts of attention, but I have my doubts that this will change in the future, because the players that do continue to play are the ones who get the most out of the current structure of the game. Everyone else simply stops playing, effectively throwing those twenty dollars in the trash.
If I could get a refund at this point, I probably would. Instead, I may just end up building my own, balanced version of this emerging game genre, and I will do so under a free and open source license. You shouldn’t expect people to pay for something that isn’t even finished (or good), as they have no measure of the actual value that product has, or will have.
In summary, don’t buy RUST unless you like being constantly frustrated and picked on, or you are willing to suck the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥of whatever admin is currently running the server you are playing on.

Chest, our neighbor from down the road, warned us of the incoming invasion. As they ran by his house, the admin had told him that he had 7 people coming. Seven! I thought there was no way it was going to be more than 4. Tobit kept tabs on the parameter, keeping an eye out for our first sighting. Meanwhile, me and Dream began preping in our houses. Chest had made his way to the gate. The raiders opened fire on Chest but Dream came out and retrieved him, hiding him away in the house. Now we're all posted up in our houses. Two of them blow through our forward gate and move behind a shack for cover. We start trading fire from our houses for a while but, eventually, all 7 raiders rush to Dream's house and quickly blow in the 1st floor. Bad move. Of all our houses, Dream's is the most akin to a labyrinth.
Over the next 2 hours, they clawed their way through Dream's house. Tobit sniped through windows until the bandits put barriers in front of the windows after a couple close calls. I tried to sneak behind them but I got lost in Dream's house and spotted. After I was gunned down, I respawned in my house, grabbed my spare m4 and headed to my roof to fire at them through some of the windows on my side of Dream's house. During one of the bandit rushes on the rooms, Chest gets picked off, but Dream manages to slip deeper into his house. The raid goes on for so long, several members of the raid begin to complain and want to just leave, despite not looting anything of value. When we caught wind that they might be leaving, Tobit set up right outside of Dream's house. They were out of c4 and sick of using grenades so they finally began funneling out of the house. It was pitch-black as they left, and they weren't expecting a sudden hail of shotgun rounds from Tobit.
When the dust cleared, 3 bodies laid at the bottom of dream's house (1 from the spike walls, 2 from Tobit's gunfire). 3 in the house (Me, Chest and a raider who had commited suicide). I have been debating on whether to buy Rust or DayZ for a few weeks now.  I've read through many pro/con discussions regarding Rust vs. DayZ. Where DayZ seems more zombie centric, Rust has more of the survival/scavenging/crafting aspect that I find more entertaining.
I bought it last night, zoned in, started hitting things with my rock to collect materials. Collected a bunch of wood, like almost 400 logs. Then I started hitting rocks to get stones, I pounded on those boulders for a long time, nothing happened. That's when I realized that I had to find nodes and not just the mountain rocks.  By this time I was already down to 800 on my food, so I set off to find critters to kill and eat.  I'd like to say my first life in Rust didn't end with me wandering around, dying from starvation, but I'd be lying.  Rust is unforgiving, and mistakes early on can lead to an agonizing death.
Next life, I zone in and I'm instantly attacked by both a wolf and a zombie.  Dead. Sometimes it's not the choices you make, but the choices you're handed that decide your fate.
Next life, I wander around and find some friendlies who give me clothes, a bow, food, cloth, and tons of starter stuff. Awesome, I'm not starving, have a shelter and starting to carve out a life for myself when I'm out hunting and I'm attacked from behind by a zombie. Dead again.
I respawn and try to get back to my corpse so I can pick up my newly acquired loot, I'm totally lost but finally manage to get to a landmark that I recognize.  I'm near starving when I get to my backpack when, yeah that zombie that killed me is still nearby and he eats my naked, cold newb self.
Next life, I give up on the backpack. Back with my rock in hand, I get my logs and my stones, build myself a shack and campfire inside, but I'm still hungry.  I set out, trying to sneak up on pigs and deer, manage to get a couple whacks at a deer but it runs too close to what I think is a bear. I let it go, and focus on the piggy.  Here piggy piggy piggy. I flail wildly, trying to land a blow on the pig, but I keep missing. It's getting dark. I'm down to 600 food, hungry and cold.  But finally, after about five minutes of chasing that little bugger, a very satisfying, wet thwack of my hatchet hits paydirt! I start butchering the pig, getting animal fat, chicken breast (?), and cloth, glorious cloth!
I make it back to my shack, fumble with trying to get the food on the campfire, accidentally eating raw chicken and getting poisoned.
Throwing up, food down to under 200 now as I get it on the fire. Not only am I starving, but I'm poisoned and losing health.  Health hits 65, waiting.  Throw up some more, health at 50.  I'm watching the fire, waiting for it to be done, I'm starving, I need it, I need it to survive when... it's cooked!  Oh the glorious pixels of cooked chicken breast harvested from a pig that I ran down and killed with a hatchet! A hatchet that I made! I munched down on it, watching my health and hunger start to climb. I could almost taste it, and the glorious satisfaction of bringing myself back from the brink of starvation was so rewarding. I ate enough to fill my health and food completely, sitting next to my fire during the night, cozy, listening to footsteps outside and gunfire in the distance. I would not be dying today. I was going to make it to tomorrow.
At sunrise I'm up. I had enough cloth to make a bow, and enough stones/wood to make some arrows. I made quick work of the deer that eluded me yesterday, harvesting food, logs, and minerals at ever opportunity.  I didn't venture far from my campsite, both in fear of losing my way back to camp and running into undesirables.  I made clothes, a sleeping bag, some fuel, and cooked up a mess of chicken, and built a storage bin in my shack to hold my inventory just in case I wander out and get killed I'll still have a stockpile out there I can find.
Eventually I found some friendlies again who gave me some supplies, more cloth, some blueprints, nothing too far up the food chain but things I could eventually use when I decide to go on the offensive against the zombies.  But nothing in game was as satisfying as surviving that first night, making that first kill, and setting myself up with a sustainable campsite.
Other bonus is I'm on a PVE server, which is awesome for learning the game. Everyone is friendly, so you don't have to worry about griefers shotgunning your naked self while you've only got a rock.

Rust is an online adventure role-playing game made from the developers of the hit game Garry’s Mod. This game is all about survival, trying to survive against animals, zombies, and other players to build a grand house, cook chicken, make alliances, and hunt others. Rust shows a lot of potential for only being an Alpha development game...
Rust’s graphics won’t win any awards, however they get the job done presenting a barren, and lonely landscape. Fields of grass, rocks, cliffs, bordering up to the southern ocean with a road going around the center of the map, where most of the action happens. By the road there are several radiation towns, and zombies around them. The models aren’t anything special. There’s a few basic animals that look decent, two types of zombies which look less than decent (however the developers plan to take them out). There is currently only one player model that is just a basic human (type “censor.nudity false” in console to see nude men!). Overall the environments and models are average, and very Unity-esc. There are few graphical options to the game currently, at startup you can select from a few basic options, and in the main menu you can change the render distance and vsync. However by typing commands in console you can change options like turning grass off (there is a great guide to this
). Hopefully in the future they will add more graphical options and optimize the game more.
Survival games aren't exactly brand new to the industry. However each game has it’s own unique play style and feel to it, and Rust is no exception. You have a set amount of calories and need to continually eat so that you don’t starve.There is also your general health which can deteriorate from attacks from players, wolves, bears, fall damage, hunger and other factors. The last state is your radiation state, which is how much radiation you have from walking around radiation towns and such. There’s no set objective in the game, other than to survive, however many players make many goals than just surviving.  In the beginning the player starts out only with a rock, bandages, and a torch. From there you have to hit trees to get wood, and hit certain kinds of rocks to get rocks, metal ore, and sulfur ore. Once you have enough wood, you can build a shelter, which will act as a temporary base. Then you’ll want to go animal hunting and try to find a deer or pig to kill with your rock. Hunting in this game is very tedious in the beginning of a player’s life and can be exceptionally frustrating for a new player. You try to chase the animal around attempting to hit it with your rock while trying to run and watch out for other threats. If you were to eventually kill an animal, then in order to get the cloth, raw chicken breast, animal fat, and blood from it, you have to hit it with your rock for about another minute. While all of these things seem tedious by themselves, they all somehow give an odd sense of accomplishment when successful. Now you can make a campfire to cook your chicken, and make a sleeping bag for a spawn point. The developers have recently introduced a cot  as well, which is a nice addition than just a sleeping bag. Eventually you’ll be able to make a larger, and custom house which is a very nice feature. This is where a lot of people have fun with Rust. People can build huge mansion like houses, or gigantic towers seen from miles away. But all of these come with the people who want to take them and all of the loot inside. Building an impenetrable house is almost impossible, however this is where another aspect of the most fun is, which is raiding. Get a group of friends together, gear up and take a house down, loot all of the stuff, kill the people inside and run away victorious. However you might have just started a war. This just adds another level of depth to this game. In order to get items in the game (other than raiding or killing other players) there are a few ways. The first ways is to craft it with the craft menu, this usually takes refined metal, wood, and other materials which are used together to make things like hunting bows, revolvers, and windows for your house, as well as many other things. However not everything can be crafted right out of spawn, you have to pick up some things from zombies or Rad towns. Zombies contain many different items including blueprints to how to make more complex things like rifles. you can also find these things in Rad towns. Rust gameplay is unique from other games as well as difficult and tedious, however extremely rewarding.
Rust is solely multiplay, and I believe that the developers will keep it that way. The Rust community can be brutal and many will kill on sight, resulting in you having to respawn countless numbers of times in your early game. However Garry himself puts it best when other players don’t kill you “It's a weird thing. When any player can kill you easily - and they don't, it's like the biggest compliment ever. They become good friends. You go to bed, and lie there and think to yourself "that was a nice guy, I hope I run into him again." Garry is 100% true about this, it is one of the things that really push this game along (however be warned you will die A Lot). Most of the servers are good and mid-low ping, however they will occasionally wipe with updates, and servers go down when there is a new update until they update, making you wait for long periods of time until the admin gets on to update it.
Garry and his team really work hard on this game and push out updates quickly, and are working to fix things that are problems, constantly optimizing the game, squashing bugs, and banning banners. The game however has experienced DDos attacks in the past, but the team worked diligently and got the servers back up.
Rust is an extremely fun game if players outlast the beginning noobiness of just starting out. Only being in Alpha stage development, the game has the potential to be one of the most popular games of all time. This game definitely deserves a look from anybody moderately interested in the concept, there are some great videos online that I suggest you take a look at.This will prove to be another one of Garry’s masterpieces.

I have been debating on whether to buy Rust or DayZ for a few weeks now.  I've read through many pro/con discussions regarding Rust vs. DayZ. Where DayZ seems more zombie centric, Rust has more of the survival/scavenging/crafting aspect that I find more entertaining.
I bought it last night, zoned in, started hitting things with my rock to collect materials. Collected a bunch of wood, like almost 400 logs. Then I started hitting rocks to get stones, I pounded on those boulders for a long time, nothing happened. That's when I realized that I had to find nodes and not just the mountain rocks.  By this time I was already down to 800 on my food, so I set off to find critters to kill and eat.  I'd like to say my first life in Rust didn't end with me wandering around, dying from starvation, but I'd be lying.  Rust is unforgiving, and mistakes early on can lead to an agonizing death.
Next life, I zone in and I'm instantly attacked by both a wolf and a zombie.  Dead. Sometimes it's not the choices you make, but the choices you're handed that decide your fate.
Next life, I wander around and find some friendlies who give me clothes, a bow, food, cloth, and tons of starter stuff. Awesome, I'm not starving, have a shelter and starting to carve out a life for myself when I'm out hunting and I'm attacked from behind by a zombie. Dead again.
I respawn and try to get back to my corpse so I can pick up my newly acquired loot, I'm totally lost but finally manage to get to a landmark that I recognize.  I'm near starving when I get to my backpack when, yeah that zombie that killed me is still nearby and he eats my naked, cold newb self.
Next life, I give up on the backpack. Back with my rock in hand, I get my logs and my stones, build myself a shack and campfire inside, but I'm still hungry.  I set out, trying to sneak up on pigs and deer, manage to get a couple whacks at a deer but it runs too close to what I think is a bear. I let it go, and focus on the piggy.  Here piggy piggy piggy. I flail wildly, trying to land a blow on the pig, but I keep missing. It's getting dark. I'm down to 600 food, hungry and cold.  But finally, after about five minutes of chasing that little bugger, a very satisfying, wet thwack of my hatchet hits paydirt! I start butchering the pig, getting animal fat, chicken breast (?), and cloth, glorious cloth!
I make it back to my shack, fumble with trying to get the food on the campfire, accidentally eating raw chicken and getting poisoned.
Throwing up, food down to under 200 now as I get it on the fire. Not only am I starving, but I'm poisoned and losing health.  Health hits 65, waiting.  Throw up some more, health at 50.  I'm watching the fire, waiting for it to be done, I'm starving, I need it, I need it to survive when... it's cooked!  Oh the glorious pixels of cooked chicken breast harvested from a pig that I ran down and killed with a hatchet! A hatchet that I made! I munched down on it, watching my health and hunger start to climb. I could almost taste it, and the glorious satisfaction of bringing myself back from the brink of starvation was so rewarding. I ate enough to fill my health and food completely, sitting next to my fire during the night, cozy, listening to footsteps outside and gunfire in the distance. I would not be dying today. I was going to make it to tomorrow.
At sunrise I'm up. I had enough cloth to make a bow, and enough stones/wood to make some arrows. I made quick work of the deer that eluded me yesterday, harvesting food, logs, and minerals at ever opportunity.  I didn't venture far from my campsite, both in fear of losing my way back to camp and running into undesirables.  I made clothes, a sleeping bag, some fuel, and cooked up a mess of chicken, and built a storage bin in my shack to hold my inventory just in case I wander out and get killed I'll still have a stockpile out there I can find.
Eventually I found some friendlies again who gave me some supplies, more cloth, some blueprints, nothing too far up the food chain but things I could eventually use when I decide to go on the offensive against the zombies.  But nothing in game was as satisfying as surviving that first night, making that first kill, and setting myself up with a sustainable campsite.
Other bonus is I'm on a PVE server, which is awesome for learning the game. Everyone is friendly, so you don't have to worry about griefers shotgunning your naked self while you've only got a rock.

Update 2015 (Almost two years later): I put maybe another 80 hours into the game about 8 months ago, and a lot has changed since my initial review. The game has a new engine and has been revamped from the ground up. Rust probably has the most impressive realistic building system on the market now, and is pretty decent in terms of being a shooter. They are including new items, systems, and features into the game on a monthly basis.
With cheaters being under control now, the game is really blossoming. The developers wipe server progress every month now, so all your in-game possessions and buildings will be wiped clean, but you will retain the blue-prints you've learned that allow you to build unique items. Rust will get better and better into the future; the gameplay is unique with building, survival, and FPS elements being rolled into one game perfectly. I think this game will take off once it launches, and will soon be ported over to consoles. It's a shame, though, that Facepunch is moving so slowly in developing it. I've owned this game several years now and have seen it grow tremendously, but it's still a long way from being finished.

It's rough around the edges, but all diamonds start that way. Here is my tale:
I have a nice, hidden base in a valley rich in resources. I had just gotten back from killing zomies and scavenging a radiation drenched town, when I decided to see if I could map out my surroundings a little. Well, the neighbors are trapped in a huge struggle with a guy in a face wrap wielding a P250. I snuck my way along the rocks around the edge of the house and tried to creep around the edge to see if I'd been followed and was consequently sprayed to death.
I respawn in my base, grab a bow and some arrows along with a hatchet and take off in a different direction. I'm stalking a buck, brimming with raw chicken breasts, when a hail of bullets showers down upon me and get me bleeding. I duck behind a rock, bandage, then take off. I stop short and dive into a cranny as the guy rips past me. I run the other way and head back to base. This huge pile of wood stopped me dead in my tracks as I furiously hammered away with my hatchet. Lo and behold, hail of bullets is back! I load my bow up and shoot the guy in the arm before taking off around a corner. I duck behind the corner into another nook (seriously, phenomenal collision detection) as the guy takes off past me. Hey, hail of bullets, meet arrow to the kneecap. Guy had killed almost all of my neighbors after a long day's work. I was rich.
It starts off slow. Spawn in a field, run around hitting trees and, if you're lucky, stones with your rock. You chase down a pig and smack it a couple times with your rock. Some naked guy with an M4 sprays you down. You spawn in a forest just as a huge plane roars over head, showering big air drops attached to parachutes. One lands right in front of you! Except you're on the ground because some desperate lunatic shot you with a jury rigged pipe shotgun.
You spawn in a field and start running. Night has come and you're very....cold...You're stomach lets out a loud growl and the sun sinks slyly over the last hill. The moon is gorgeous and rising. You bump into a rock. No, that's a wolf. You spawn by a coast and heft your rock. You smash it against a dark stone that is standing awkwardly in a field. Somehow, you get a few stones and gather some wood by banging said rock against trees. Now you make yourself a stone hatchet. That guy with the pipe shotgun got an MP5A4 from that air drop and tells you to crouch. *Sigh* you do it. He tells you directions and marches you up a steep rock face and has you jump along cliffs. You peer over and see various drop points all the way down to various stages of death. His friend opens a door and a bunch of other new players walk over to the cliff at shotgun point. They tell us to pay bullseye. The only platform that looks remotely survivable has a shelter on it. That's what we're aiming for.
We jump. Most of us die. You survive with 2 others, but sustain severe injuries. They throw you supplies. They throw you makeshift handcannons and some ammunition. You understand. You grab them and kill one of the others while they question it. The other guy is fumbling long enough for you to kill him, too. The guy with the MP5 shoots you.
You spawn in a forest near a zombie. You manage to kill it with your rock. He has a bolt action rifle on him that's loaded. A big plane roars overhead and, to your luck, drops a big package right near you. You run over and make it there as it lands. A shirtless guy holding a rock is laughing in the mic and going through it. He spawns in a field.

Suprisingly, Rust is a beautiful and amazing game for such an early alpha (cough, *dayz*, cough). The game is quite easy to pick up and play but also manages to stay quite complex, with many weapons, armour, building materials and items to craft. The graphics are great and not too system intensive. This game is great to play on your own, or with friends. When you are on your own Rust feels like a truly immersive survival experence and when with friends it is fun to try and start your own clan and defend and attack other players and bases.
There are some downsides however which i will now list:
- FPS drops form time to time (i guess this depends on your PC build but I have a 650 ti if youre wondering)
- It can be quite frustrating to build your own little empire and then with one shot you lose it all. Some people may like this as it encourages caution, but take that for what you will.
- As it is still in alpha their are some bugs and glitches (getting stuck in rocks, animals disappearing etc.)
- From time to time you may run across hackers, which is extremely frustrating and unfair. (developers are working hard to completely eliminate this however.)
Overall, I find this game extremely enjoyable and plan to keep playing it in the future and I can't wait to see what the developers bring to the table as development continues.

Update 2015 (Almost two years later): I put maybe another 80 hours into the game about 8 months ago, and a lot has changed since my initial review. The game has a new engine and has been revamped from the ground up. Rust probably has the most impressive realistic building system on the market now, and is pretty decent in terms of being a shooter. They are including new items, systems, and features into the game on a monthly basis.
With cheaters being under control now, the game is really blossoming. The developers wipe server progress every month now, so all your in-game possessions and buildings will be wiped clean, but you will retain the blue-prints you've learned that allow you to build unique items. Rust will get better and better into the future; the gameplay is unique with building, survival, and FPS elements being rolled into one game perfectly. I think this game will take off once it launches, and will soon be ported over to consoles. It's a shame, though, that Facepunch is moving so slowly in developing it. I've owned this game several years now and have seen it grow tremendously, but it's still a long way from being finished.

It's rough around the edges, but all diamonds start that way. Here is my tale:
I have a nice, hidden base in a valley rich in resources. I had just gotten back from killing zomies and scavenging a radiation drenched town, when I decided to see if I could map out my surroundings a little. Well, the neighbors are trapped in a huge struggle with a guy in a face wrap wielding a P250. I snuck my way along the rocks around the edge of the house and tried to creep around the edge to see if I'd been followed and was consequently sprayed to death.
I respawn in my base, grab a bow and some arrows along with a hatchet and take off in a different direction. I'm stalking a buck, brimming with raw chicken breasts, when a hail of bullets showers down upon me and get me bleeding. I duck behind a rock, bandage, then take off. I stop short and dive into a cranny as the guy rips past me. I run the other way and head back to base. This huge pile of wood stopped me dead in my tracks as I furiously hammered away with my hatchet. Lo and behold, hail of bullets is back! I load my bow up and shoot the guy in the arm before taking off around a corner. I duck behind the corner into another nook (seriously, phenomenal collision detection) as the guy takes off past me. Hey, hail of bullets, meet arrow to the kneecap. Guy had killed almost all of my neighbors after a long day's work. I was rich.
It starts off slow. Spawn in a field, run around hitting trees and, if you're lucky, stones with your rock. You chase down a pig and smack it a couple times with your rock. Some naked guy with an M4 sprays you down. You spawn in a forest just as a huge plane roars over head, showering big air drops attached to parachutes. One lands right in front of you! Except you're on the ground because some desperate lunatic shot you with a jury rigged pipe shotgun.
You spawn in a field and start running. Night has come and you're very....cold...You're stomach lets out a loud growl and the sun sinks slyly over the last hill. The moon is gorgeous and rising. You bump into a rock. No, that's a wolf. You spawn by a coast and heft your rock. You smash it against a dark stone that is standing awkwardly in a field. Somehow, you get a few stones and gather some wood by banging said rock against trees. Now you make yourself a stone hatchet. That guy with the pipe shotgun got an MP5A4 from that air drop and tells you to crouch. *Sigh* you do it. He tells you directions and marches you up a steep rock face and has you jump along cliffs. You peer over and see various drop points all the way down to various stages of death. His friend opens a door and a bunch of other new players walk over to the cliff at shotgun point. They tell us to pay bullseye. The only platform that looks remotely survivable has a shelter on it. That's what we're aiming for.
We jump. Most of us die. You survive with 2 others, but sustain severe injuries. They throw you supplies. They throw you makeshift handcannons and some ammunition. You understand. You grab them and kill one of the others while they question it. The other guy is fumbling long enough for you to kill him, too. The guy with the MP5 shoots you.
You spawn in a forest near a zombie. You manage to kill it with your rock. He has a bolt action rifle on him that's loaded. A big plane roars overhead and, to your luck, drops a big package right near you. You run over and make it there as it lands. A shirtless guy holding a rock is laughing in the mic and going through it. He spawns in a field.

Suprisingly, Rust is a beautiful and amazing game for such an early alpha (cough, *dayz*, cough). The game is quite easy to pick up and play but also manages to stay quite complex, with many weapons, armour, building materials and items to craft. The graphics are great and not too system intensive. This game is great to play on your own, or with friends. When you are on your own Rust feels like a truly immersive survival experence and when with friends it is fun to try and start your own clan and defend and attack other players and bases.
There are some downsides however which i will now list:
- FPS drops form time to time (i guess this depends on your PC build but I have a 650 ti if youre wondering)
- It can be quite frustrating to build your own little empire and then with one shot you lose it all. Some people may like this as it encourages caution, but take that for what you will.
- As it is still in alpha their are some bugs and glitches (getting stuck in rocks, animals disappearing etc.)
- From time to time you may run across hackers, which is extremely frustrating and unfair. (developers are working hard to completely eliminate this however.)
Overall, I find this game extremely enjoyable and plan to keep playing it in the future and I can't wait to see what the developers bring to the table as development continues.

I spawned with nothing but a rock, torch and bandages to get me by. I met someone who looked very similar to myself, 'maybe we could be twins?' I thought, we both had the bald head, pale complexion, must be.. We teamed up, pooling our resources and hunting as one. Mining wood, sulphur, stone and metals we managed to form a furnace, just big enough to refine our ores. Next came metal fragments, gun powder and eventually what we called: the hand cannon.
We felt unstoppable, like the love-children of Bear Grylls and Minecraft, we roamed the land in search of a more permanent home. Somewhere to hang our coat for the night and rest peacefully. After long, arduous hours a small village was erected, storage boxes fabricated and weapons stored. 'This is it' we thought, 'we've made it'. However, it just wasn't enough. We began looting sleeping settlers, smashing in wooden doors like they were made from polystyrene, just to get the 'next best thing'. Destroying sleeping bags so no one would know where they were, once they regained consciousness of course.
This was our downfall. The beginning of the end.
As our greed grew, so did our village. We needed more barricades to keep people out, but with the barricades came more attention, with more attention came more noise. We would wait for people in the night, wait for them to seek out our village or 'maze of doors' as we liked to call it, and strike. Their bows, arrows and hatchets were nothing against the mighty pipe shotgun.
One day, we ventured too far and 'knocked' on the wrong door. Greeted by an M4 and P250 we fled into the wilderness.
It was too late.
'Not to worry, we'll just respawn at the village, in our sleeping bags!' - Or so we thought... 'It must be a problem with our respawns, try again so we can finally return home!' - Nothing.
Panicking, we ran, ran as fast as we could, our stamina running out fast and not a cooked chicken breast in sight, radiation filling our bodies and zombies biting at our heels. 'I've found it! I'm home!' my partner cried in joy, 'oh, hang on a sec..'
The village was empty, the doors destroyed, the shotguns were gone and materials looted. We had become victims of our own paths. What we had done, was done unto us.
This is our story.
(Serious bit)

Rust most defintely plays out in a different direction than its current survival competitor: DayZ.  Instead of scrounging materials to survive in the shells of old residences, you harvest materials for construction in much the same way as you do in the king of all survivals: Minecraft. However, instead of digging a hole and holding out against creatures of the night, instead you build a residence or fortification and begin to carve a space out as your own within the different valleys. The main difference comes about with playing this game with a friend or two and working to build a community together. You are allowed to build structures and fortifications, but are limited to the size and scope of your buildings through the placement of your foundations. As a result, if you are aiming to achieve a stylized look or feel to your town, working with some friends will get crafting and building done much faster. Definitely recommended as a great exercize in communal planning and collaboration, but this comes with a caveat. Although the large majority of players are looking to be your friend or do their own thing, there are always a few people in the servers looking to grief new players.

You spawn in half naked. Your only worldly possessions is a rock, torch, bandages and a snack. Then you manage put together some basic cloth clothes; killed a hog and got uncooked chicken; gathered some ore and wood; built a camp fire and settled down in your basic shack/shelter for the night in your comfy sleeping bag. The next morning you wake up in an unfamiliar place in the middle of a grass field. You're naked. Lost everything you owned. And you're left wondering what happened last night.
It's like a bad acid trip in real life.
That'll sum it up for most new players who at least make it through the first night and have not been killed in the first few hours. Climbing the Rust Evolutionary Latter is something that most players are going to have to do more than once until they get the hang of the game or until they've managed to form alliances with other players. It sounds like a bad review so far.. but I love this game. Here's why:
It's PvP/PvE and like most PvP games the majority of veteran players are going to be the ones that make it hard for new players to get established-that's just the nature of most PvP gamers. But once you start to get established, built a nice fort with some defences and formed an alliance or two it starts to take off. You feel an attachment to the creation you built. You start to collect resources feverishly to replenish your stores and to build even bigger. While exploring and collecting resources you are always keeping a mental note of good places to build a second compound that's better hidden and with better natural defences. Single player right now is fine. But co-op is where it starts to shine-if you can manage form alliances. Cooperation with other players to help build your compound; defending; resource planning (limited to simply "what is more important to build right now" at least) and expansion is much more fun than roughing it alone.
And that's where the rub is with new players that can't find the fun in the game. Because they're either playing on an official server that are filled with griefers, roving bandits and just general unfriendly players who shoot on site (I admit I've done it once or twice... a few times). Or are on a community server with a shady admin. The trick is to find that gem of a server with a decent admin, low enough population where most of the players aren't obnoxious kids who think they're playing CoD still.
RUST is going to be what you make of it and how fair the Admins are. Yes there are improvements to be made and some flaws-but it's an Alpha. The developers can only do so much to try to control player behaviour. And you can only blame the game so far because in the end it's just that there's so many bad players and they are everywhere-no matter what game when it comes to an MMO.
And that's where I am with the current server I am playing. F1 > net.connect
I'm not an admin there but I'm hoping that the majority of people who will and are currently playing are of the level headed type. So far so good. Only the occasional skirmish, robberies and retaliatory raid to keep things interesting.

You spawn in half naked. Your only worldly possessions is a rock, torch, bandages and a snack. Then you manage put together some basic cloth clothes; killed a hog and got uncooked chicken; gathered some ore and wood; built a camp fire and settled down in your basic shack/shelter for the night in your comfy sleeping bag. The next morning you wake up in an unfamiliar place in the middle of a grass field. You're naked. Lost everything you owned. And you're left wondering what happened last night.
It's like a bad acid trip in real life.
That'll sum it up for most new players who at least make it through the first night and have not been killed in the first few hours. Climbing the Rust Evolutionary Latter is something that most players are going to have to do more than once until they get the hang of the game or until they've managed to form alliances with other players. It sounds like a bad review so far.. but I love this game. Here's why:
It's PvP/PvE and like most PvP games the majority of veteran players are going to be the ones that make it hard for new players to get established-that's just the nature of most PvP gamers. But once you start to get established, built a nice fort with some defences and formed an alliance or two it starts to take off. You feel an attachment to the creation you built. You start to collect resources feverishly to replenish your stores and to build even bigger. While exploring and collecting resources you are always keeping a mental note of good places to build a second compound that's better hidden and with better natural defences. Single player right now is fine. But co-op is where it starts to shine-if you can manage form alliances. Cooperation with other players to help build your compound; defending; resource planning (limited to simply "what is more important to build right now" at least) and expansion is much more fun than roughing it alone.
And that's where the rub is with new players that can't find the fun in the game. Because they're either playing on an official server that are filled with griefers, roving bandits and just general unfriendly players who shoot on site (I admit I've done it once or twice... a few times). Or are on a community server with a shady admin. The trick is to find that gem of a server with a decent admin, low enough population where most of the players aren't obnoxious kids who think they're playing CoD still.
RUST is going to be what you make of it and how fair the Admins are. Yes there are improvements to be made and some flaws-but it's an Alpha. The developers can only do so much to try to control player behaviour. And you can only blame the game so far because in the end it's just that there's so many bad players and they are everywhere-no matter what game when it comes to an MMO.
And that's where I am with the current server I am playing. F1 > net.connect
I'm not an admin there but I'm hoping that the majority of people who will and are currently playing are of the level headed type. So far so good. Only the occasional skirmish, robberies and retaliatory raid to keep things interesting.

Since I first played Rust back in January 2014, I knew it was a game destined for greatness. An online survival game that revolutionise the survival genre. Since then I have forgotten about Rust. The legacy branch was placed in the back burner and the glitchy, buggy mess that was Experimental took the lead. Since I left Rust, Facepunch Studios have been actively developing it, adding new content and fixes every week. One day Rust returned to my attention and I decided to see if it had surpassed its old roots [legacy.]
And it has. Big time!
The new Rust is completely unrecognisable from the old. Nearly everything about it was overhauled and redone from scratch, and it makes full use of the Unity engine to deliver a paramount and absolutely georgeous experience not found in any other online survival game of this kind. Whereas Rust's original rivals such as DayZ have fallen into the shadows and others have taken its place, Rust has continued to stay strong developing a strong and loyal community of fans as well as becoming one of the most unique, original and memorable online survival experiences on Steam. For the sake of this review, I will refer to the old Rust using the term Legacy Rust.

This is of course a survival game, so how does the survival factor affect your gameplay? This time around, Facepunch have put greater emphasis on the PvE aspect adding in different biomes with their own unique temperatures. If you're in the winter biome at night, you will freeze to death, if you're in the desert biome in the day, you will burn to death. Unlike Legacy, where the only major threats (aside from players) were hunger, the incessant wolves and radiation, now you have to worry about thirst and temperature. These added dynamics add greater depth to the environment and add a greater challenge. Furthermore, the infamous NPC animals make their return and are made from scratch utilising better AI and animal-specific meat (Bears and wolves no longer drop chicken breast.)
Of course, no online survival game is complete without its psychopathic inhabitants, a.k.a the players. This aspect remains virtually the same as Legacy.

Combat has always been a major part of any online survival video game. It is the primary vessel for gathering resources from NPCs, hunting others and defending yourself or just for entertainment. It is well known that Legacy Rust's combat was incredibly unbalanced. Those who wore full kevlar and used an M4 had an incredibly big advantage over their enemy and in most cases were unstoppable Now, this advantage has been taken away with the complete overhaul of weapons and how they are used. The higher-tier weapons such as the AK and shotgun are far more harder to find and craft, leaving the Thompson (successor to the MP4A5), the handcannon, the bow and various others. To combat this, Facepunch also implemented better melee weapons including a bone knife and a throwable spear. This gives starting players a better chance for hunting and protection without needing to scour a rad town to get a weapon like in the old days because let's face it, melee in Legacy Rust was a joke.

The visual aspect of Rust is what impressed me the most. The first time I tried new Rust out, I spawned close to a snow biome and I was just breathtaken at the beauty. It is definetely a great looking game that makes use of Unity better than Legacy. There is more vivid colour, lush vegetation and better looking forests. In comparison to Legacy, this is where New Rust has changed the most.
On ultra settings, Legacy Rust didn't look too bad and had a sort of rustic charm to it. However it lacked any real colour as the dominant colour in the Rust world was a yellow-ish colour, something you'd see in Breaking Bad.
As for design, everything looks just like it's meant to. Clothes are no longer mere patches of colour to distinguish armour type, but proper great-looking apparel. It all looks crudely-made and savage. Weapons are no longer professional-looking but look the part: Duct-taped, made of wood and stone and covered in scratches and bumps as if they were made by a bald psychopathic man.

Rust is an online survival game that is definetely worth checking out. If you hold your doubts because of Legacy Rust, throw them away. This is an entirely different game that is constantly being added to thanks to its active developers and a strong loyal fanbase. I hope to see even greater things from Rust in the future.

I regret picking this game up. There are basically three resources that I've come across. Rocks, trees, and animals. And each of these resources give out three or four different items. The idea of the game is to survive, but so long as you don't get stuck in a zone with no animals at all, like I did, you can pretty much survive with utter ease, the only real threat being other players.
Once you get guns, though, other players tend to leave you alone. You've won the day! Now what to do with all your free time?
I don't know, talk in world chat maybe? It's hard to feel alone and desperate for survival when people can communicate across the world in order to trade/sell items, call in for back up, or just chat.
Since I got bored of "survival" I tried to go the Minecraft route of just making things, with my ultimate goal of making a bridge or tower to unreachable places in order to make a huge beacon fire... but I found that incredibly limiting given the tools I had. (The fact that I kept dying because I couldn't find animals for food and bed didn't help this either)
I bought it, and thus I'm stuck with it, but I hope in a year or so, maybe there will be something akin to role play servers with no world chat, and increased difficulty to get guns, or something to actually do.
Edit:
Also... The inherent goal of "survive" really doesn't mean a whole lot when death isn't much more than an inconvenience. There aren't any consequences to death... and as it stands, I don't even know how you could implement any.

If you're trying to decide whether your money is better spent here, or DayZ ; BUY THIS GAME, IT'S MORE COMPLETE.
Here are some reasons why :
Now, this game has ALREADY given me hundreds of hours of awsomeness, despite it being in alpha.
Let me give you a comparison, I have 285 hours on Rust, and 9 on DayZ at the time of this review.
This is NOT because DayZ is a bad game. But it's simply because what Garry Newman (Creator of Rust & Garry's mod) has brought to the table, has all of its elements complete. What I mean by this, Is all of the mechanics are working currently. There's no gamebreaking bugs. No character's disappearing, no zombies running through walls/gates/doors like in DayZ standalone.
Also, In my opinion Rust has a lot more promise than DayZ. Garry has said he is not trying to make Rust "like every other zombie game" So, he's going to be replacing the zombies soon with something hopefully more interesting. Also, you can  build your own bases in Rust! A fort if you will, to fend off any invaders that try and ransack it.
In this game you will also never find yourself running around for 4 hours only to find nothing. Instead, you can craft all your tools/guns. You can start on a new server, run into a radtown, and if you get lucky there could be a gun in the very first crate you search. Or go hit a couple rocks with your rock, then some trees, build a furnace, and slam yourself together a Revolver!
Another cool thing about the crafting, is the ability to research objects you can't craft. So say you just killed somone for their full set of Kevlar armor (The best defensive equipment in the game) But you want to learn how to research it, so that you can craft it yourself. To do this, you will need to kill zombies in Radtowns to find Research Kits. You can use these on an object and it will teach you how to craft it. Taking away from the need to kill zombies for the Kevlar armor blueprints. (Rarer spawn than kits) Because often times then not, it will be easier to ambush someone in kevlar, than harvest it yourself.
I'm gonna keep this review short, all in all Rust is an amazing game so far, with incredible things to be added soon, (Cars, Helicopters, Different armors/Building materials.)
I would definitely recommend it over DayZ if you're trying to make up your mind.

My first impression of Rust wasn't favorable. It seemed (at first glance) to be a low budget free-roamer with more style than substance. I am so glad i was wrong.
Rust has a charm that draws you into the world and after a bit of a learning curve (which isn't steep) you will be surviving and raiding like a pro. While still in early alpha the game shows great promise for those that love open-world survival.
In my opinion the main appeal of rust is how it effortlessly ramps up the tension and gets your heart pumping.
Waiting out the night in a crude shack with little more than a rock for protection is a intense experience. You are never sure if that sound you just heard outside is man-made or not. Do you wait til dawn or go out in the dark to see what made the noise? Do you even leave your house for fear of raiders? Do you carry your best gear to give yourself a edge or hide it to ensure if killed your corpse won't be looted? These questions will have you pacing the floor of your home in rust, armed to the teeth and jumping at shadows.
The intensity is sadly intirely dependent on how many players are on any given server. Therefore more players equals more potential allies, enemies and victims.
In short this game is well worth the money as long as the few hackers i have seen are properly banned before the finished product is released

This is a simple review for a currently simple game.  You start with the basics, a rock, 2 bandages to stop bleeding, and a torch that lasts 250 seconds.  You will first beat a tree for wood, then a rock for metal to obtian a hatchet.  Then you will make a small shelter for surviving the dark night.  Then you will hunt for food if you are still alive, and potentially get lost on your travels.  The map is big, and there are very few landmarks.  You must survive based on your ability to remember locations, or get lost trying to get home.
Once you get the guns you want, and the armor you can use to survive luxuriously in, you have nothing left to do.  The journey can be fun, but once you'v ehit the destination, you're done.  Unless you enjoy hunting those weaker then you, there is no replayability.
Building is also a pain.  Wood is the basic building tool, and you require thousands of it to get enough building foundations and planks to build a fortress.  Then there is the lack of ability to remodel your home.  You do something wrong, tough, you can't fix some of your mistakes, making your home less "homely".  Unless you can build perfectly the first time, it's less than comfortable to spend your precious foundations, walls, and columns.
This game is in the Alpha, and will be better, I'm sure.

Rust is basicly:
the crafting from Minecraft,
the building mechanics from DayZ Epoch,
and the weapons from Garry's Mod.

I've been in game long enough to hear people say it's a human ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly simulator, and it's just that.
If you came to this game looking for a fun and simple survival experience, a way to relax while progressing your way up the tech trees and building a place to call home.. then you are in the wrong place.
This is a survival game, it's going to be difficult.
This is a game with tech trees, you retain your knowledge of blueprints you find and can build new weapons or buildings.
This is a game where survival is important if you want to keep all of your stuff.
This is a game where working with others... is optional.
Where i'm getting with this is that by all means this is a survival game in it's mechanics, however the playerbase makes it something different.
I want to ask the readers of my review if they have ever played Garry's Mod, have you? If you have then you would know that in many servers without death protection there is trolling beyond belief, spawn killing, spawn trapping, and in general just people being douches.
"But Svarr, not every server in Rust is like that, not everyone is a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" -- Yes this is true, there are some servers that disable player VS player combat and those generally tend to be a little friendlier in terms of death count.. However there is a mechanic in Rust so that your buildings you place CANNOT BE REMOVED EASILY IF AT ALL AND CAN BE PLACED MOSTLY ANYWHERE, EVEN NEAR OTHER PEOPLE'S BUILDINGS, yes, you can even place a wall in front of a door to block people from getting in or out, thus ruining everything they have done for those long and difficult hours they have been playing. That's all it takes.
If you play this game you have a very high chance of wasting your time doing so, yes wasted, why would i use that word? Because everything you have done in game is gone the moment someone decides to troll you, and that happens often. The only thing kept is your blueprints you have learned, that's it.
*So let's describe how a regular game of PVP Rust before the PVE Rust experience.*
PVP Start: You spawn in world and see a bunch of crudely built shacks from the starter blueprint, this server has a mod to give you starter items so you type in /starter and recieve a stone axe, basic shelter, camp fire, and stove. Good start so far to get things rolling!
Some few minutes later while you are gathering wood a player comes by and shoots you in the back of the head for a one hit kill, oh dear, you just died and they had nothing to gain from it, you were pretty much nude and helpless in the starting area. Oh well, at least you can start again and try to go out a bit more, right? They did loot your body but you can just get that again.
You spawn in again and run out a bit, it's dark out and you can hardly see anything, but this allows you to get away without being seen, all you have is a rock (gathering tool somehow) and a torch. This time you are near the ocean in the cliffs, you see many more abandoned homes that are falling apart constantly, some of the walls falling down from decay.. You figure you'll be safer among old rotting huts that have already been ransacked many times over, at least for now.
You try using the /starter command again in order to get a head start but to no avail, it appears it can only be used once only 40 minutes and you are stuck with only a rock and torch, if you use your torch you'll meet a most certain death as player-killers will see it for miles and come to you with a shotgun and a full suit of Kevlar armor, so instead you try to get wood in the dark, you gather enough wood for a door which you put on one of the huts you found without a door so you would not have to make your own hut, you feel safer now as you have your own room, small as it may be.
You find yourself getting hungry and need to find food, you have not seen any animals nearby slow enough to catch, deer are too quick to catch on foot, bears will murder you without a gun, wolves will make you bleed to death from their bites, and pigs are your only resource left, so your only choice is to try and find a pig in the morning, you notice your hunger bar also has a cold status, you could start a campfire but then players would find and kill you, you decide to freeze for tonight, and figure you might have to get used to it.
Morning is coming along and you figure you should hunt while the sun is rising so you are still slightly under cover of darkness, at least to just scout it out first. You cannot build a bedroll to respawn in your hut without cloth, and to get cloth you kill ... pigs, for some reason, as any other animal. You try to use your /starter command again, but cannot yet. You are starting to starve and must get food quickly. Quietly edging around cliff sides in a meadow you try to spot players to avoid or food to catch, you spot no animals, you spread out for a while and still find nothing and fear that if you go out any further you'll lose sight of your home so you keep trying to roam nearby. You could easily get sniped from here with scoped weapons so you decide to hurry it up and risk it by running.
You keep roaming around for a while unable to find food nearby, you die of hunger before you can find any, yes just like that.
You re-do everything you done before and this time you could use /starter again, you decide to hoof it as fast as possible to avoid dying like before, put up your hut, build a door from some wood real quick, and this time you made sure to find a place with food this time.
You feel set! You have food properly this time nearby, some resources of stone and wood, you feel like a king once you collect enough stuff! You start to get better at sneaking around and gathering under the radar, you got your friend on to the server and he's helping you out at your home, you find out how to build after messing up the first time, you have yourself a warm home to call yours, two stories high and the day endling irl. You decide to go to bed and log out your character in the server while inside your virtual bedroom. Things are going well and you plan to play again after your real life responsibility of work or school, or being with friends.
The next day when you log on to the server you are surprised and disappointed when you find your doors blown off their hinges by explosives or destroyed by pickaxes! You've only been gone one day you think, how could this have happened? Do i really need to stay in game ALL the time to keep anything i've built or done? My character is even dead and looted, the same for my friend... Why would this happen to me? Damn it.
If you decide to continue, you may get a little bit luckier but meet the same end the next day, if not, you quit and go to another server and have the same thing happen once more, if you join a server that does not allow player vs player combat then read the next segment.
PVP story end.
--
PVE Start: You log on to a PVE server and convince your friend to join you there instead, he was convinced to keep trying on the last one but joined you anyway, that's good, things move faster with friends.
You start building and the community seems okay so far here, some random religion or politics discussion going on, internet things as normal. Having built up your house with your friend everything seems fine, no threats, no problems. You read online that if you leave the server without using anything in your house like a door or fireplace then your place will start to decay, so you plan with your friend to get on every day at night and make this your regular game.
As you both log out and sleep irl some guy places a wall in front of your only door out and ruins it all, you quit the game out of fusteration and never come back. The end.
PVE story end.

My first impression of Rust wasn't favorable. It seemed (at first glance) to be a low budget free-roamer with more style than substance. I am so glad i was wrong.
Rust has a charm that draws you into the world and after a bit of a learning curve (which isn't steep) you will be surviving and raiding like a pro. While still in early alpha the game shows great promise for those that love open-world survival.
In my opinion the main appeal of rust is how it effortlessly ramps up the tension and gets your heart pumping.
Waiting out the night in a crude shack with little more than a rock for protection is a intense experience. You are never sure if that sound you just heard outside is man-made or not. Do you wait til dawn or go out in the dark to see what made the noise? Do you even leave your house for fear of raiders? Do you carry your best gear to give yourself a edge or hide it to ensure if killed your corpse won't be looted? These questions will have you pacing the floor of your home in rust, armed to the teeth and jumping at shadows.
The intensity is sadly intirely dependent on how many players are on any given server. Therefore more players equals more potential allies, enemies and victims.
In short this game is well worth the money as long as the few hackers i have seen are properly banned before the finished product is released

This is a simple review for a currently simple game.  You start with the basics, a rock, 2 bandages to stop bleeding, and a torch that lasts 250 seconds.  You will first beat a tree for wood, then a rock for metal to obtian a hatchet.  Then you will make a small shelter for surviving the dark night.  Then you will hunt for food if you are still alive, and potentially get lost on your travels.  The map is big, and there are very few landmarks.  You must survive based on your ability to remember locations, or get lost trying to get home.
Once you get the guns you want, and the armor you can use to survive luxuriously in, you have nothing left to do.  The journey can be fun, but once you'v ehit the destination, you're done.  Unless you enjoy hunting those weaker then you, there is no replayability.
Building is also a pain.  Wood is the basic building tool, and you require thousands of it to get enough building foundations and planks to build a fortress.  Then there is the lack of ability to remodel your home.  You do something wrong, tough, you can't fix some of your mistakes, making your home less "homely".  Unless you can build perfectly the first time, it's less than comfortable to spend your precious foundations, walls, and columns.
This game is in the Alpha, and will be better, I'm sure.

I tried out rust on a few practice servers before joining a community one and really trying. The chances are that every now and then,your first spawn will be next to a zombie. My friend spawned for the first time next to three rocks, one wood pile and a zombie, couldn't fight off the zombie and died instantly. Just today, before I could even see, I spawned next to the stronger type of zombie and died before I could move.
However! Don't let this put you off, as on your third spawn or so, things are looking up! My first two days have just been completed today (45 minute days and 15 minutes night times in case you were curious) and on my first night, I spawned in near-pitch black. My recommendation if this happens is to go as close to the nearest small shack as possible, you can sometimes even stay warm. Once it was morning, I was able to get enough wood to make my own tiny wooden shack, pretty close to supply spawn points. The best thing to do in this game is make friends. Without friends, you will die. A very helpful player called Hypno was helping myself and another (presumably) noob. We were even given supplies and a place to sleep for the night. Don't be afraid to ask for help, sometimes you can get some awesome stuff.
For an Alpha game, this is really well developed and it's very realistic and generally awesome. I get a lot of lag on my computer, but other than that, I highly recommend Rust! I've already gotten many friends to download it too!
Be warned that as of now, you can't connect to a server from Mac, but you can get Bootcamp for Mac and run Windows on Mac, which is what I have done to play Rust.
Keep up the great work guys!
